New research, coauthored by Western University biology professor David Coltman, identifies genetic factors that help lodgepole pines survive mountain pine beetle attacks.
## Pinecones offer clues to lodgepole resistance
The mountain pine beetle is native to western North America, but its most recent population explosion has been unprecedented in scale. Since the late 1990s, the outbreak has affected more than 27 million hectares (67 million acres) of forest across Canada, the United States and northern Mexico.
"When a mountain pine beetle bores into a tree, the tree responds by producing resin. It's both a chemical defense and a physical one," said Coltman. "The resin can push the beetle back out, trap it and potentially kill it. It forms a little tube around the point of attack, almost like a tree scab."
Researchers collected cones from trees that survived the outbreak and those killed by beetles, then planted the seeds and grew the young trees under the same conditions. Cones from surviving trees were collected near the ends of branches, where seeds were likely to have been fertilized by other surviving trees. The findings also suggest the beetle outbreak itself has changed the genetic makeup of surviving lodgepole pine tree populations. Researchers found evidence of reduced genetic diversity at most of the sampled sites, alongside genetic signatures associated with survival.

Those genetic differences may help explain why some trees are better equipped to defend themselves against an attack.
When beetle populations grow large enough, as has happened across North America, the insects can overwhelm even healthy trees through mass attack. They also introduce a fungus that helps them colonize the tree and contributes to its death. The fungus causes the blue staining sometimes found in beetle-killed pine timber.

## Abstract
Taking advantage of lodgepole pine cone serotiny, we collected cones from MPB-killed and MPB-survivor maternal trees to establish a common garden of their progeny to investigate the genetic architecture that is associated with host survival.
We genotyped 418 progeny at 14,267 loci and used population, quantitative and landscape genomics to investigate (i) the extent to which severe MPB outbreaks influence genetic diversity of lodgepole pine, (ii) whether progeny of lodgepole pine survivors from a hyperepidemic have different genetic signatures than progeny of MPB-killed lodgepole pine, (iii) the heritability of pine survival of these MPB outbreaks, and (iv) patterns of spatial variation in
genomically-predicted pine survival of MPB outbreaks.

We observed significant reductions in lodgepole pine standing genetic diversity at most sampled sites. Through genomic selection and genome-wide association analyses we identified loci that differentiated progeny of MPB-survivor and MPB-killed trees. Spatial mapping of polygenic survivorship scores shows broad enrichment for predicted survival in the MPB endemic range, with regions of elevated predicted survival also in the expanded range.
This study provides evidence that MPB exerts selection pressure on lodgepole pine genotype, and that natural regeneration of lodgepole pine from survivors may increase the genetic variation associated with reduced MPB host quality.

On its own, the mountain pine beetle hardly seems a menace. No larger than a grain of rice, it is often the victim when it tries to burrow into a towering pine, killed by the tree’s natural defenses.

  But let that beetle call over some friends, and watch out. Acres of trees can fall in their wake. In British Columbia, where pine beetle populations are exploding, the insects have already killed nearly half of lodgepole pine trees in the province’s central forest, and they’re claiming new territory each year. Authorities now say the beetle outranks wildfire or logging as the greatest threat to the Canadian forest.

  What accounts for such deadly teamwork? Kenneth Raffa, an entomology professor who has studied mountain pine beetles for 30 years, says the insects use a kind of jujitsu, harnessing a tree’s natural chemical defenses to send out a welcoming beacon to other beetles. If enough respond, they can overcome their host’s resistance, turning it instead into a nursery for their eggs. As they bore deep inside, the beetles leave a trail of microorganisms that cut off the tree’s nutrient supply, choking it to death.

  But Raffa is also interested in the effect of forest management practices, such as decisions to thin forests or suppress wildfires. keenable.title: Effects on Genetic Architecture From Mountain Pine Beetle Mortality in Lodgepole Pine
keenable.snippet: The most recent mountain pine beetle (MPB) [Dendroctonus ponderosae Hopkins (Coleoptera: Curculionidae: Scolytinae)] epidemic caused substantial lodgepole pine (Pinus contorta Dougl. ex Loud. var. latifolia) mortality in western North America over the past three decades. Taking advantage of lodgepole pine cone serotiny, we collected cones from MPB-killed and MPB-survivor maternal trees to establish a common garden of their progeny to investigate the genetic architecture that is associated with host survival. We observed significant reductions in lodgepole pine standing genetic diversity at most sampled sites. Through genomic selection and genome-wide association analyses we identified loci that differentiated progeny of MPB-survivor and MPB-killed trees. Spatial mapping of polygenic survivorship scores shows broad enrichment for predicted survival in the MPB endemic range, with regions of elevated predicted survival also in the expanded range. This study provides evidence that MPB exerts selection pressure on lodgepole pine genotype, and that natural regeneration of lodgepole pine from survivors may increase the genetic variation associated with reduced MPB host quality.

keenable.title: Mountain pine beetle spread in forests with varying host resistance
keenable.snippet: In the last few decades, mountain pine beetle (MPB) have spread into novel regions in Canada. An important aspect seldom captured in models of MPB spread is host resistance. Lodgepole pine, the predominant host of MPB, varies in resistance across the landscape. There is evidence for a genetic component of resistance, as well as evidence that hosts in areas where MPB has not been present historically are at risk of increased susceptibility. In addition to the spatially varying resistance of the primary host species, the eastward spread of MPB has brought them into jack pine forests. Host resistance in jack pine remains uncertain, but experiments indicate jack pine could be a suitable host. We develop a model of pine beetle spread that links pine beetle population dynamics and forest structure and resistance. We find that beetle outbreaks in the model are characterized by large transient outbreaks that move through the forest. We show how the speed of these outbreaks changes with host resistance and find that biologically plausible values for host resistance are able to stop the wave from advancing. We also find that near the threshold of resistance where the wave is able to advance, small changes in host resistance dramatically decrease the severity of the outbreak. These results indicate that planting trees selected for higher MPB resistance on the landscape may be able to slow or even stop the local spread of MPB. In terms of further eastward spread, our results indicate future outbreaks may move more quickly and be more severe if novel lodgepole pine hosts are indeed more susceptible to beetle attacks, although more research is needed into the susceptibility of jack pine.

## Abstract

In the last few decades, mountain pine beetle (MPB) have spread into novel regions in Canada. An important aspect seldom captured in models of MPB spread is host resistance. Lodgepole pine, the predominant host of MPB, varies in resistance across the landscape. We also find that near the threshold of resistance where the wave is able to advance, small changes in host resistance dramatically decrease the severity of the outbreak. These results indicate that planting trees selected for higher MPB resistance on the landscape may be able to slow or even stop the local spread of MPB. In terms of further eastward spread, our results indicate future outbreaks may move more quickly and be more severe if novel lodgepole pine hosts are indeed more susceptible to beetle attacks, although more research is needed into the susceptibility of jack pine.
